questions.question_text: Which is a valid declaration of a double variable?
questions.explanation: A double holds decimal values: double x = 3.5;. Assigning 3.5 to an int loses the decimal (or won't compile); a String literal and boolean are type mismatches.

questions.question_text: What is the value of 17 % 5?
questions.explanation: Modulus returns the remainder: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2, so 17 % 5 = 2. The quotient (3) is what / would give; modulus gives what's left over.

questions.question_text: After int a = 5; double b = a;, what is b?
questions.explanation: Widening an int to a double is automatic and produces 5.0. No cast is needed going from a smaller to a larger numeric type; the reverse (double to int) requires an explicit cast.

questions.question_text: What does "RACECAR".indexOf("CE") return?
questions.explanation: indexOf returns the starting index of the first match. In R(0)A(1)C(2)E(3)C(4)A(5)R(6), the substring 'CE' begins at index 2. indexOf returns the START position, not the end.

questions.question_text: What does "hello".length() return?
questions.explanation: length() counts characters: h-e-l-l-o = 5. Note length() is a METHOD for Strings (with parentheses), while arrays use the length FIELD (no parentheses) — a frequent mix-up.

questions.question_text: Integer wrapper objects: what does Integer.parseInt("42") + 1 produce?
questions.explanation: parseInt converts the String "42" to the int 42, then + 1 gives 43 (numeric addition). If it stayed a String, + would concatenate to "421" — parsing is what enables arithmetic.

questions.question_text: What does this print? int x = 7; if (x % 2 == 0) System.out.print("even"); else System.out.print("odd");
questions.explanation: 7 % 2 = 1, which is not 0, so the else branch runs → 'odd'. The modulus-equals-zero test is the standard even/odd check.

questions.question_text: Which condition is true only when x is between 1 and 10 inclusive?
questions.explanation: A range check needs && (both must hold) with inclusive operators. Option A/C use || (almost always true); option D isn't valid Java syntax for chained comparison.

questions.question_text: If a is false, in (a && b), what happens to b?
questions.option_b: b is not evaluated due to short-circuiting
questions.explanation: With &&, if the left operand is false the whole expression is false, so Java skips evaluating b (short-circuit). This is used to guard against errors like null checks before method calls.

questions.question_text: How many times does this print? for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) System.out.println(i);
questions.explanation: i = 0,1,2,3,4 — five iterations; at i = 5 the condition i < 5 fails. Starting at 0 with < 5 is the standard idiom for exactly 5 repetitions.

questions.question_text: What is the sum after: int s=0; for(int i=1;i<=4;i++) s+=i;
questions.explanation: Adds 1+2+3+4 = 10. The loop runs for i = 1,2,3,4 (inclusive due to <=), accumulating each into s.

questions.question_text: What does a nested loop 'for(i=0;i<3;i++) for(j=0;j<2;j++) count++;' leave count as?
questions.explanation: Inner loop runs 2 times for each of the 3 outer iterations: 3 × 2 = 6. Nested loop counts multiply, not add — a key insight for 2D traversal.

questions.question_text: A constructor is a special method that:
questions.option_b: initializes a new object and shares the class's name with no return type
questions.explanation: Constructors share the class name, have no return type, and set up initial field values when 'new' creates an object. They aren't static and don't return values.

questions.question_text: An accessor (getter) method typically:
questions.option_b: returns the value of a private field without changing it
questions.explanation: Accessors return field values to support encapsulation (private fields, public access). Mutators (setters) change fields. A getter that's void couldn't return anything — contradiction.

questions.question_text: Encapsulation is best achieved by:
questions.option_b: making fields private and providing controlled access via public methods
questions.explanation: Encapsulation hides internal state (private fields) and exposes it only through controlled methods, protecting invariants. Public fields break encapsulation by allowing uncontrolled external changes.

questions.question_text: How do you access the first element of int[] arr?
questions.explanation: Java arrays are zero-indexed, so the first element is arr[0]. There's no first() method, and parentheses aren't used for indexing — square brackets are.

questions.question_text: What does int[] a = new int[3]; initialize its elements to?
questions.explanation: Java auto-initializes numeric array elements to 0 (booleans to false, objects to null). Unlike some languages, Java arrays never contain uninitialized 'garbage.'

questions.question_text: To find the maximum in an int array, you should initialize max to:
questions.option_b: the first element of the array
questions.explanation: Starting max at arr[0] handles arrays with all-negative values correctly. Starting at 0 wrongly returns 0 for an all-negative array — a classic bug the exam tests.

questions.question_text: Which correctly adds "cat" to an ArrayList<String> list?
questions.explanation: ArrayLists use add() to append elements; there's no append() method, and bracket indexing works on arrays, not ArrayLists. Use get()/set() for indexed access on a list.

questions.question_text: What does list.size() return for an ArrayList?
questions.option_b: the number of elements currently in the list
questions.option_c: the index of the last element
questions.explanation: size() gives the current element count. Note arrays use .length (field), Strings use .length() (method), and ArrayLists use .size() (method) — three different conventions to keep straight.

questions.question_text: To safely remove all even numbers from an ArrayList<Integer> while iterating, you should:
questions.option_a: use a for-each loop and call remove()
questions.option_b: iterate backward by index, or use an Iterator's remove()
questions.explanation: Removing during a forward index loop skips elements (shifting), and modifying during a for-each throws ConcurrentModificationException. Iterating backward or using Iterator.remove() avoids both.

questions.question_text: For int[][] grid = new int[2][3], how many total elements are there?
questions.explanation: A 2×3 array has 2 rows × 3 columns = 6 elements. Multiply the dimensions; adding them (5) is the common error.

questions.question_text: What does grid[1][2] access in a 2D array?
questions.option_b: row index 1, column index 2 (second row, third column)
questions.explanation: 2D arrays are [row][column], both zero-indexed: [1][2] is the second row, third column. Treating the indices as 1-based positions is the usual mistake.

questions.question_text: The keyword 'super' in a subclass is used to:
questions.option_b: call the superclass's constructor or methods
questions.explanation: super invokes the parent class's constructor (super(...)) or overridden methods (super.method()). It lets a subclass reuse and extend parent behavior rather than fully replacing it.

questions.question_text: If class Cat extends Animal, which statement is valid?
questions.explanation: A subclass object can be stored in a superclass reference (a Cat IS an Animal). The reverse (Animal into Cat) needs a cast and isn't generally valid; the other options are type errors.

questions.question_text: Method overriding requires the subclass method to have:
questions.option_b: the same name, parameters, and compatible return type as the parent method
questions.explanation: Overriding replaces a parent method with a matching signature (same name and parameters). Changing the parameter list is OVERLOADING, not overriding — a distinction the exam tests.

questions.question_text: Every recursive method must have:
questions.option_b: a base case that stops the recursion
questions.explanation: Without a base case, recursion never stops and causes a StackOverflowError. The base case is the condition under which the method returns without calling itself.

questions.question_text: int sum(int n){ if(n==0) return 0; return n + sum(n-1);} What is sum(3)?
questions.explanation: 3 + sum(2) = 3 + 2 + sum(1) = 3 + 2 + 1 + sum(0) = 3+2+1+0 = 6. The base case (n==0 returns 0) stops the recursion and the additions unwind.

questions.question_text: A recursive method that calls itself with the same argument every time will:
questions.option_b: never reach the base case and cause a StackOverflowError
questions.explanation: Recursion must move toward the base case (e.g., n-1). Calling with an unchanged argument loops forever, exhausting the call stack — the most common recursion bug.
